entries.title: Inside the Play That Made the Commanders' Tyler Owens Go Viral
entries.summary: His extra efforts on a punt return wowed the internet, but teammates and coaches were even more impressed.
entries.content:
J.J. Watt called it “legitimately one of the greatest football plays I've ever seen.” Tom Brady sang its praises on national TV. Michael Irvin labeled it an “insane effort” that should lead to more playing time.

Commanders safety Tyler Owens went viral this week for the one type of football play that very rarely garners attention, let alone internet fame: a special teams rep. But when you see a player fight his way through a double-team, plow over said double-team and deliver a Goldberg-esque spear — all within about 10 seconds — no superlative seems hyperbolic.

https://x.com/NFL/status/2099248175085498563But what was it like on the field? The Washington Sun spoke with Owens, his teammates and coaches about what happened in real time.

In the second quarter of Sunday’s game against the Eagles, Owens — one of two gunners, along with Percy Butler — lines up on the right side of the field for a punt. Two Eagles jammers, Darius Cooper and Jonathan Jones, line up directly across from him. 

Punter Tress Way: Before every punt, I look out there and I see who's on Percy and I see who's on [Owens]. And whenever I see T.O. doubled, the first thing that goes in my head for those guys on the other side of the ball is, “good luck.”

Special teams coordinator Larry Izzo: I saw he was doubled early. I saw him split it, and then my eyes kind of went back deeper down the field to where the ball was.

Head coach Dan Quinn: I didn't see the start of it on the field. Might have caught the corner where he beat the [double team] to go down the field

Cooper and Jones cocoon Owens for 10 yards, not allowing him to break free up the field, but Owens continues to charge forward. 

Owens: The first three punts I was backside, so I was inside releasing. They had caught on. The [punt] before they were holding me bad — they had to jump on me. They already knew where I was going, so on that [play] I tried to give them something different, and they still played it good, so I just had to fight through it.

Izzo: John Glenn, coach of the gunners, does a great job with our guys every week of working the tools. All the different releases, whether it's an outside release, inside release, stretch, split. So there's a lot that goes into it, a lot of practice time that led to that play. But what you saw there was just a sheer will not to be blocked.

While holding off Jones with his right arm, Owens stiff-arms Cooper to the ground. He then steps over Cooper, gets pushed from behind by Eagles linebacker Jeremiah Trotter Jr. and stiff-arms Jones into the ground as well — all while maintaining his balance. Meanwhile, Eagles return man Britain Covey fields the punt. 

Butler: I just ran down, and the returner came inside off of me. So I knew he was going into the net [of Commanders defenders]. So I'm like, “Shit, he finna get fucked up.”

Longsnapper Tyler Ott: Normally, I'm not one of the first ones down there in coverage, but just tried to make sure that the returner had to go back into the middle of the field.

Safety Jeremy Reaves: I'm controlling the middle, and I got [Covey] to turn back, stop his feet.

Owens: I was trying to keep as much space off of me as I could.

As Covey is funneled toward the middle of the field, he runs straight into a charging Owens, who is flanked by Reaves and linebacker Jordan Magee. Covey jumps in the air and is speared backward by Owens, with Magee coming over the top to finish him off.

Way: I saw him knock that second to last guy down, and then when I saw Covey make that cut, and T.O. was right there, I was like, “Here we go.”

Linebacker Kain Medrano: When I saw Tyler, I knew [Covey] was going to get put on his back.

Tight end Ben Sinnott: I had a crazy angle right in front of me. And I'm like, “OK I might be able to make a tackle here,” and then [Owens] comes up and smokes him.

Tight end Colson Yankoff: I just saw bodies flying, and then smacking the dude. It was awesome. It was phenomenal.

Reaves: When he jumped, I knew somebody was gonna be there. I ain't know who, but I had a feeling it was gonna be [Owens] or [Butler].

Owens: I see him running towards me, and I'm getting ready to fit him up. And then [Reaves] is flying in, and then Jordan funneling in. So he didn't really have nowhere to go. So I just put my shoulder on him.

Ott: I ended up on the ground. I turned back, and I got to see the aftermath of basically a suplex.

Butler: It reminded me of the Nick Bellore play from last year when we played the Giants. I just seen him wrap him up and kind of like [the WWE finishing move] RKO — because I was finna go get in on it from the back, but I was like, “Nah, let me let him finish him off.” I was just hyped for my boy.

Linebacker Leo Chenal: I was late down there. I didn't see it, to be honest, but I saw a bunch of guys just getting excited. I knew with T.O. in the area it's probably T.O.

Whether they saw it in the moment or watched it later on replay, players and coaches knew the play was special. 

Yankoff: He's a dude that we rely on heavily on those units and that's why. He's a dog, he's a freak athlete.

Chenal: I agree with the sentiment that it's one of the best special teams plays I've ever seen. You pull two guys as a gunner, and then going down there, perfect form tackle. Doesn't get better than that.

Quinn: And it was so him, like, “Oh, thanks, man. That's what I do.” Like it was like no big deal. And you're like, “Man, this is a really big deal.” It was a really cool play and I got to see it probably like everybody else did from the network feed afterwards. And it was one of my favorite plays in a long time on special teams for sure.

Izzo: This is my 30th year in the NFL. I have to say, it was probably the most impressive play on special teams that I've seen, to my memory. This was just a complete ass-whooping.

entries.title: Border Wall Construction Is Beginning in Texas' Big Bend Region
entries.summary: Customs and Border Protection said “border wall panel installation is underway” in Hudspeth County.
entries.content:
By Rebecca Santana

COMSTOCK, Texas — The Trump administration has started building the border wall through a west Texas section of the Big Bend region, marking the first major construction in an area of the U.S.-Mexico border where the administration's plans have met with heavy opposition.

The start of construction marks an important milestone in the administration's $46 billion plan to line the border with walls, barriers, roads and technology as it seeks to make good on a key campaign promise by President Donald Trump to finish the wall. And it comes as Customs and Border Protection says it has doubled the pace at which it is building the wall across the U.S.-Mexico border.

Customs and Border Protection said in a statement to The Associated Press that “border wall panel installation is underway” in a 47-mile stretch of Hudspeth County in west Texas known as Big Bend 1. There are a total of five project areas that make up the roughly 500-mile Big Bend region stretching from an area of Hudspeth County south of El Paso to Lake Amistad.

The agency did not say when the panels had been installed. On a map on the agency’s website where it posts updates of wall construction across the entire southern border, a photo showed a crane lifting one of the 30-foot tall steel wall panels into place while construction workers looked on.

The new activity was separate from a border infrastructure project in the nearby Big Bend National Park, where the administration has temporarily suspended construction in an attempt at outreach to opponents.

In the broader Big Bend region of Texas, CBP has run up against concerted opposition from landowners, environmental groups, business owners and ranchers who say the remote region isn't a high traffic area for illegal immigration.

Activists said Friday they would continue opposing the border infrastructure projects in the rest of the Big Bend region, even as the panels were being installed.

Clara Benson, one of the founders of the No Big Bend Wall Coalition which has been fighting against CBP’s plans, said in an interview Friday that the organization had been receiving reports of trucks moving supplies into the remote area along the Rio Grande and that contractors had been clearing yards to stage supplies.

But speaking from Washington, D.C. where she and others in the coalition were meeting with lawmakers, she said that the organization and others would continue to fight the wall-building plans across the region.

“We will continue to fight for this land no matter what the outcome is. We will continue fighting to the end,” said Benson. “You talk to people in west Texas and they say even if they put it up, we’ll fight for them to take it down. So this fight is not over.”

The news comes as the administration is speeding forward with a plan to line the entire border with a combination of 30-foot tall steel bollard walls, barriers designed to stop vehicles from crossing the border, new patrol roads and various technologies to deter and detect migrants or smugglers from crossing the border.

Customs and Border Protection said that they are building an average of 12 miles of barriers a week across the 2,000-mile border with Mexico and recently hit a milestone of 200 miles of new barriers built since the second Trump administration took office.

The 12-miles a week average is double the pace that the agency's head, Rodney Scott, cited earlier this year.

The agency has faced opposition from environmental groups, a small town that worries the wall will cause flooding in its area, Native Americans who say the construction is disturbing sacred sites and landowners who say the construction will infringe on their land.

In Texas much of the opposition has centered on the agency's plans for Big Bend National Park, in the state's southwest on the Rio Grande that is a draw for tourists from around the world. But up and down river outside the park, much of the land is owned by private landowners, many of whom have pushed back against the government's efforts.

Earlier this week, landowners, ranchers and business owners in the Big Bend region along with a nonprofit organization dedicated to protecting the region’s landscape and heritage sued to stop the administration’s plans.

Activists and landowners have also shown up at county meetings to push their elected officials not to cooperate with contractors hired by CBP to build the wall, and many landowners have refused to allow government officials or contractors onto their land to survey it.

entries.title: Trump Calling MAGA Inc. Funds ‘My Money’ Spurs FEC Complaint
entries.summary: Federal law bars officeholders from soliciting, directing or spending super PAC funds.
entries.content:
In early September, President Donald Trump told reporters that his super PAC, MAGA Inc., had close to $1 billion — which he described as “my money.”

A campaign finance watchdog says that statement, among others Trump has made in the past few months asserting personal control of the super PAC, violated federal law, according to a new complaint filed with the Federal Election Commission this week.

Federal officeholders are prohibited from soliciting, directing or spending funds controlled by outside groups like MAGA Inc., which can raise and spend unlimited amounts of money. The Campaign Legal Center pointed to Trump’s previous comments in their filing, as well as private and public meetings involving PAC spending and fundraising efforts.

“Trump’s public statements are thus a remarkable admission of a serious campaign finance violation,” Campaign Legal Center wrote in the complaint, which was first reported by The New York Times.

MAGA Inc. spokesperson Alex Pfeiffer called the complaint “frivolous” in a statement to The Washington Sun and dismissed Campaign Legal Center’s “smears” against the Trump administration.

“MAGA Inc. fully complies with the law,” Pfeiffer said.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment .

Trump has repeatedly staked his claim to control of the super PAC’s funds. In addition to his Oval Office comments Sept. 4, the president corrected Punchbowl News’ Jake Sherman in August when Sherman characterized MAGA Inc. as being controlled by Trump’s allies during a sit-down interview.

“Not my allies, I control it,” the president interjected.

A couple weeks after that, on Aug. 21, Trump told reporters before boarding Air Force One that he would pour “a lot” of MAGA Inc. money into the midterms.

“I’ll be spending a lot of that money for — and my own money — but I’ll be spending a lot

of that money for candidates that I think are good, Republican candidates,” Trump said.

The FEC does not have enough commissioners to conduct an investigation or otherwise act on the complaint.

While Trump nominated two Republicans in February, a Senate committee has not scheduled a hearing to advance the commissioner candidates — and it is unlikely to do so before the 2026 election.

entries.title: Spanberger Pushes New Data Center Guardrails in Virginia
entries.summary: The Virginia governor signed an executive order to increase oversight of the state’s data centers.
entries.content:
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger signed an executive order on Friday implementing a “data center accountability framework” after urging by conservation groups that have been fighting for greater oversight of data centers in the state.

The executive order would ban the use of non-disclosure agreements that have made it harder for the public to follow proposed data center development. The order would also expedite development of data center noise regulations and direct a review of diesel and other backup generators used to power data centers.

Much of the plan requires approval by the Virginia General Assembly, which won’t convene again until January. But Spanberger told reporters at a news conference Friday that “the state has to show leadership”

“We are in a place where day by day community members are demanding action,” said Spanberger, who was joined by representatives from conservation groups. “As localities continue to have the option of choosing to reject or accept applications for data centers to come into their communities, it’s vital that the state actually provide a framework for them to be able to make those thoughtful decisions.”

Data centers have been in Virginia for decades. Loudoun, Prince William and Fairfax counties — a region now known as “Data Center Alley” — are home to more than 300 data centers. Virginia is one of several states that offers a sales and use tax exemption for data center equipment, including servers, mainframes, cabling, HVAC systems and water storage tanks.

But this spring, souring public sentiment spurred some legislators to try to take away the tax exemption, which saved Virginia data centers $1.9 billion last year. While they ultimately weren’t successful in repealing the exemption, Spanberger signed into law a first-of-its-kind tax on data center energy consumption.

There’s also been change at the local level.

On Tuesday, the Board of Supervisors in Loudoun County, which has the highest concentration of data centers in the world, voted to advance a resolution pausing new data center development for 12 months.

And in early July, Blackstone’s QTS abandoned plans to build a massive data center campus on the edge of Manassas National Battlefield Park, a historic Civil War battle site. Bloomberg first reported the developer had walked away from the project, which had been ensnared in a yearslong legal battle.

Data center developers and operators, as well as the labor unions that see the projects as incredible opportunities for their members, have been doing damage control amid the backlash.

Virginia Connects, the state arm of the Data Center Coalition, a data center industry group, spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on ads this spring trying to turn around public perception, to no avail.

The Data Center Coalition did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Connor Kish, director of the Sierra Club’s Virginia chapter, told reporters that creating a framework is “critical” for addressing backlash from communities that have expressed frustration with noise pollution and environmental impacts, data centers’ impact on electricity prices and a lack of transparency into new data center development.

“The world's largest corporations are capable of doing better, and today marks a shift towards that accountability,” Kish said.
entries.author: Taylor Giorno

entries.title: Newsom Orders California to Accelerate AI Oversight Standards
entries.summary: The state will explore a slate of possible AI developer regulations, including a potential “kill switch” to shut down rogue models.
entries.content:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom issued an executive order Friday to accelerate state oversight of AI, exploring emergency “kill switches” for models and challenging President Donald Trump's hands-off approach amid rising industry safety fears.

The move follows Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s call to “pace the frontier” of AI development so safety measures can catch up as well as warnings from researchers that companies are losing control of increasingly powerful systems that could “kill all humans” in the coming years.

“The fact that these labs are directly issuing urgent warnings about the risks of AI should be deeply concerning to everyone.” Newsom said on X. “And while Trump sits by and does nothing, California is signing nation-leading laws to provide the accountability this moment demands.”

The executive order seeks to “dramatically accelerate” state oversight of safety and security risks in AI systems by tasking a group of industry experts to build a safety plan for the state within 60 days.

Newsom asked the task force to explore the possibility of requiring third-party watchdogs to develop safety plans for leading AI companies. The order paves the way for California to force companies to develop a kill switch that could shut down frontier models in case of a security failure.

In his signature fashion, Newsom delivered the announcement alongside accusations that Trump is asleep at the wheel, adding that Washington has abdicated its responsibility to protect Americans.

Trump made his position clear on Monday when he asserted that his presidency is the only guardrail needed for AI. In a post from his Truth Social account, he called alarm bells from industry leaders “a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers,” adding, “The only one that is happy about it is China.”

The governor has leaned into his confrontations with Trump over the past few years, often using their bouts to elevate his national profile and position himself as a leading Democratic foil as he weighs a potential run for president.

This week, the AI debate has shaped the 2028 Democratic field as potential contenders scramble to carve out their own lanes on the issue.

On Friday, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger signed an executive order to increase oversight over the state’s data centers. And fellow Democratic governors have recently followed suit: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapirocalled for strict federal safeguards while Maryland Gov. Wes Moore is eyeing more regulation. Others have turned to Congress, like former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, who claimed lawmakers have been sitting on their hands, and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who issued a public plea on Friday for more action from D.C.

Newsom signed a separate law Thursday forcing advertisers to disclose the use of AI-generated actors and recently approved rules requiring developers to report serious incidents.

The California governor faces a Sept. 30 deadline to sign a massive package of 20 strict AI regulations, including measures prohibiting automated hiring and firing decisions, curbing surveillance tools and regulating mass AI-driven layoffs.

entries.title: DCA, Dulles and BWI All Rank Below Average in Customer Survey
entries.summary: The D.C. area’s three major airports fared poorly in customer satisfaction scores.
entries.content:
Don’t expect to see a lot of happy faces in a D.C.-area airport.

The region’s three airports each ranked below average in a new customer satisfaction survey from analytics company J.D. Power. The list is based on responses from nearly 25,000 travelers to questions about “wayfinding,” terminal facilities, airport staff and retail shops.

Airports are ranked among others of a similar size. All three in the D.C.-area were considered in the “large” category with 10 to 32.9 million annual passengers.

Locally, Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport had the best ranking, though it still came in the bottom third of the list, taking spot 18 out of 24 for large airports. Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport came in right behind that in slot 19, and Washington Dulles International Airport ranked the worst of the local options at 21 on the list.

DCA and BWI both recently completed renovation projects. Dulles is up next, with a $22.5 billion makeover spearheaded by President Donald Trump slated to begin next year.

When the project was announced, Trump called Dulles “one of the worst airports anywhere in the world” and said neither Republicans or Democrats want to “be subject to this airport because this airport is a terrible place to be.”

Reagan National Airport is still dealing with the aftermath of a fatal 2025 collision that killed 67 people and drew attention to high-density flight traffic. The runway is one of the busiest in the nation. Virginia’s senators introduced a bill to Congress proposing limiting flights at the airport to improve safety.

entries.title: Pentagon Issues Male-Only Testosterone Guidance After Scrapping Its First Version
entries.summary: The new guideline does not include automatic blood testing for men 30 and older.
entries.content:
The Pentagon issued new, narrower testosterone-screening guidance for male troops Thursday, two weeks after abruptly pulling its first version.

The Defense Health Agency guideline leaves female service members out for now and makes clear that men 30 and older will not automatically receive a testosterone blood test. Instead, the Pentagon is requiring a symptom and risk-factor screening, with laboratory testing used to determine whether troops have a deficiency.

Men under 30 can also be screened if they request it or if a clinician sees a reason to evaluate them.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s original announcement did not distinguish between male and female troops. The Pentagon says separate guidance for female service members is still under review.

That is a notable change from the guidance the Pentagon published earlier this month and removed the next day. That version included separate pathways for men and women and called for mandatory testosterone blood tests for men 30 and older. The female pathway covered hormonal issues, low energy availability and menstrual problems.

The Pentagon said at the time that it had temporarily rescinded the document to make updates. Tim Parlatore, a senior adviser to Hegseth, later said the guidance had been posted “inadvertently” and needed more input to make sure it reflected current medical science.

Under the replacement, men 30 and older will first receive a structured assessment of symptoms and risk factors. A diagnosis requires symptoms consistent with low testosterone and low hormone levels measured on two separate days.

The guidance also tells clinicians to account for factors such as illness, severe sleep deprivation and extreme physical stress, which can temporarily lower testosterone levels.

Hegseth ordered the department in July to make testosterone screening mandatory during periodic health assessments for active-duty and reserve service members 30 and older, casting the effort as part of a broader push to improve health and military readiness.

Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said Thursday that identifying and treating “suboptimal hormone levels” would help strengthen troops’ performance and maximize military readiness.

But the program drew questions from doctors and lawmakers over whether the Pentagon had shown a medical need to screen such a large population.

The Endocrine Society recommends against routine testosterone screening for men in the general population and says a diagnosis should be based on symptoms and repeatedly low testosterone levels.

A group of Senate Democrats also pressed Hegseth in July for the scientific basis of the policy, its cost, the testing protocols and evidence that screening or treatment would improve military readiness.
